title: Foregrounding, defamiliarization, and affect: Response to literary stories
key_findings: 4 studies, 3 short stories (O'Faolain, Mansfield, Woolf) split into 77-86 segments; N = 60, 60, 48, 30
Foregrounding index (phonetic + grammatical + semantic) correlated with segment reading time (r ~ .27-.39), strikingness (~.22-.45) and affect (~.23-.33)
Effects appeared for psychology students as well as English students -> not dependent on literary training (though psych students gave lower ratings)
Model: foregrounding -> defamiliarization -> affect -> 'refamiliarizing' interpretation
practical_applications: Put one deviating phrase (sound/image) at the turning line of a 2-line dialogue: it is where readers slow down
Do not foreground every line; contrast with plain lines is what makes one line strike

title: Effects of 'literariness' on emotions and on empathy and reflection after reading
key_findings: N = 142 randomly read 1 of 3 versions of a literary excerpt about losing a child: original (high foregrounding), without imagery, without foregrounding
Original > no-foregrounding on empathic understanding after reading; original vs no-imagery not significant
Original evoked more ambivalent (mixed beauty + sorrow) emotions; reflection not affected by foregrounding
Effects on emotion during reading disappeared when trait empathy/gender were controlled; reviews prior evidence as 'inconclusive' (van Peer et al. 2007 single-line study found no emotion effect)
practical_applications: Stripping all literary texture from a sad story flattens it; keep sound + image + rhythm together, not only metaphor
Expect mixed feelings (bittersweet) rather than more intense sadness from well-made lines
limitations: One text, Dutch students and parents

title: Parallelisms and deviations: two fundamentals of an aesthetics of poetic diction
authors: Winfried Menninghaus; Valentin Wagner; Ines Schindler; Christine A. Knoop; Stefan Blohm; Klaus Frieler; Mathias Scharinger
key_findings: Across poems, humorous couplets and proverbs: higher parallelism scores (rhyme, metre, alliteration) raised comprehensibility and liking
Higher deviation scores reduced both comprehensibility and liking
Positive parallelism effects were significantly stronger than negative deviation effects; framed as prediction-error minimisation -> fluency -> liking
practical_applications: For short wise lines, parallel structure (repetition, rhyme, mirrored clauses) is the safer bet than odd/deviant wording
Use deviation sparingly and only when parallelism carries the line
limitations: Liking is not the same as being moved or remembering

title: The emotional and aesthetic powers of parallelistic diction
authors: Winfried Menninghaus; Valentin Wagner; Eugen Wassiliwizky; Thomas Jacobsen; Christine A. Knoop
key_findings: (per MPI summary) Parallelistic features intensified all measured emotion dimensions (joy, sadness, being moved, intensity, positive affect) and aesthetic dimensions (beauty, liking, melodiousness) for 40 poems
Authors note parallelism also occurs in ritual language, ads, slogans and everyday talk
practical_applications: Rhyme/repetition in a caption line likely raises felt intensity and 'melodiousness'
limitations: Only search snippet / institute summary read; design details not verified

title: Aesthetic and emotional effects of meter and rhyme in poetry
authors: Christian Obermeier; Winfried Menninghaus; Martin von Koppenfels; Tim Raettig; Maren Schmidt-Kassow; Sascha Otterbein; Sonja A. Kotz
key_findings: 17 German listeners rated 60 four-line stanzas in metre x rhyme versions, with real words and pseudo-words (480 recordings)
Rhyme raised liking, intensity, perceived and felt positive emotion; metre raised liking and intensity
Effects roughly independent; interpreted via cognitive fluency (not measured directly)
practical_applications: Spoken VO lines that rhyme or keep a steady beat are liked more - useful for TTS taglines

title: Birds of a feather flock conjointly (?): Rhyme as reason in aphorisms
key_findings: Unfamiliar rhyming aphorisms ('What sobriety conceals, alcohol reveals') judged more accurate than non-rhyming equivalents ('...alcohol unmasks')
Advantage shrank when people were told to separate poetic quality from content
Interpretation: rhyme adds processing fluency that is misattributed to truth
practical_applications: Rhyme makes a line feel truer -> ethical duty: never use rhyme to make a weak health/product claim feel true
Rhyme is fine for feelings and reflections, not for factual claims
limitations: Single paper; English; a 2019-era replication status not checked in this session

title: The emotional power of poetry: neural circuitry, psychophysiology and compositional principles
authors: Eugen Wassiliwizky; Stefan Koelsch; Valentin Wagner; Thomas Jacobsen; Winfried Menninghaus
key_findings: 27 participants listened to recited poems; all reported chills (1.33/min); goosebumps on video in 40.7%
Chills clustered at ends of lines, stanzas and whole poems; linked to direct social address (second person, quoted speech)
fMRI (n = 17): reward-related regions; nucleus accumbens active in the build-up (prechill) period
practical_applications: Put the emotional payoff at the END of the line/slide/clip, and let it be direct address ('you...')
Second line of a Mint & Tao pair should end on the key word

title: Foregrounding (Handbook of Empirical Literary Studies)
authors: Willie van Peer; Paul Sopcak; Davide Castiglione; Olivia Fialho; Arthur M. Jacobs; Frank Hakemulder
key_findings: Foregrounding = stylistic deviation and parallelism; traced from Aristotle through Russian Formalism/Prague School to an empirical turn
Qualitative (think-aloud, interviews) and quantitative (experiments, neurocognitive) lines; possible carry-over effects (e.g. critical thinking)
Many problems remain open
practical_applications: Use as the map of the field; foregrounding is two tools (deviation + parallelism), not one

title: Neurocognitive poetics: methods and models for investigating the neuronal and cognitive-affective bases of literature reception
key_findings: Reviews methods/models for literary reading; presents the Neurocognitive Poetics Model (fiction feeling hypothesis; foregrounding vs backgrounding/immersion)
Still little known about how the brain processes literary texts
practical_applications: Familiar 'background' text supports immersion; foregrounded spots trigger aesthetic attention - alternate them
limitations: Hypothesis & theory paper; critiqued (Dixon & Bortolussi 2016 comment, not read)

title: The role of processing foregrounding in empathic reactions in literary reading
authors: Giulia Scapin; Cristina Loi; Frank Hakemulder; Katalin Balint; Elly A. Konijn
key_findings: N = 78 marked 'striking' passages; Full processing of foregrounding associated with higher state empathy than Failed processing
Depth of the reader's processing, rather than devices per se, may drive empathy
practical_applications: A striking line only works if the audience has time and cues to process it (hold the slide long enough)

title: Does literariness influence negative empathy? A study on the effects of foregrounding on readers' affective and aesthetic reactions
key_findings: N = 59 read original vs stylistically flattened excerpts (Lolita, The Kindly Ones); originals raised state empathy; aesthetic appreciation partly mediated
Empathic distress unaffected by style, predicted by trait empathy
practical_applications: Supports Koopman 2016: literary texture raises understanding, not raw distress
limitations: Small N; morally extreme texts; new journal platform

title: Readers closing in on immoral characters' consciousness: Effects of free indirect discourse on response to literary narratives
key_findings: 4 studies with rewritten versions of Borowski's 'The Record'
FID raised perceived visibility of the character's inner life although information was identical; increased situational (external) attribution of the character's behaviour
Reader background (field of study) could override text effects; overall FID effects limited
practical_applications: Writing a caption in the character's inner voice (FID) rather than narrator summary makes the audience feel they 'see inside' - same facts

title: Message design choices don't make much difference to persuasiveness and can't be counted on, not even when moderating conditions are specified
key_findings: Review of 30 meta-analyses of message variations; median mean effect r = .10; narrative vs non-narrative r = .067
95% prediction intervals for 28 of 30 effects include both positive and negative values; moderators barely narrow them
Includes conclusion present vs omitted (O'Keefe 2002) among variations
practical_applications: No single stylistic rule (narrative, explicit moral, metaphor) reliably wins; test with our audience
limitations: Read ~55% of page (results + conclusions); persuasion, not aesthetic outcomes

title: Art as Technique (Iskusstvo kak priem), trans. Lemon & Reis 1965 (course reprint)
key_findings: 'Habitualization devours work, clothes, furniture, one's wife, and the fear of war'
Art exists 'to make the stone stony'; 'impart the sensation of things as they are perceived and not as they are known'
Technique: make objects 'unfamiliar', make forms difficult, increase length of perception; Tolstoy's 'Kholstomer' (horse narrator) as example
practical_applications: Describe an everyday object as if seen for the first time (e.g., glasses as 'two windows you carry')

title: Focalization (the living handbook of narratology)
key_findings: Focalization (Genette 1972) = selection/restriction of narrative information relative to a narrator, character or other entity
Zero (narrator > character), internal (= character), external (narrator < character) - Todorov formulas
Genette separates focalization from voice (who speaks); debate with Klauk & Koppe on internal focalization
practical_applications: Choose whose knowledge a caption is limited to before writing it
limitations: Read the first part of the entry only

title: In Theory: Bakhtin - Dialogism, Polyphony and Heteroglossia
key_findings: Dialogism: meaning arises between voices; each utterance answers earlier speech and anticipates replies
Polyphony (Dostoevsky): characters' voices not subordinated to the author; monologism: one consciousness absorbs all
Heteroglossia: diversity of social speech styles within one language; unfinalizability of persons
practical_applications: Tao must not be the author's mouthpiece: give Mint a reply that partly holds its ground
limitations: Expert explainer in a magazine, not peer-reviewed; Bakhtin primaries not read

title: Aesthetics of the Everyday (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Everyday aesthetics covers daily artefacts, chores, eating, walking, social interaction; roots in Dewey's Art as Experience
Debate: everyday value via defamiliarization vs. valuing familiarity/comfort itself
Negative aesthetics (boredom, mess), atmosphere, action-oriented and social aesthetics; aesthetic-ethical link
practical_applications: Mint & Tao stories can find meaning in ordinary acts (waiting for a bus, folding laundry) without making them exotic

title: The literary transaction: Evocation and response
key_findings: (per secondary summaries) Reading is a transaction (Dewey's term): the 'poem' is an event between reader and text
Efferent stance (what to carry away) vs aesthetic stance (what is lived through) form a continuum
practical_applications: Captions should invite an aesthetic stance (feel) for stories, efferent (take away) for eye-care tips - do not mix in one line
limitations: Not read; Theory Into Practice 21(4) 268-277; conceptual essay

title: Making Meaning with Texts: Selected Essays
key_findings: Teaching subject-matter is 'the transactions between readers and books'; literary experience must first be brought about
Warns against replacing the experience with facts about literature and against sentimentalising
practical_applications: Ask 'what will the viewer live through?' before 'what will they learn?'

title: The Reading Process: A Phenomenological Approach
key_findings: (per secondary sources) Gaps/blanks between textual segments invite the reader to make connections; 'tempt' the reader onward
Contrasted with Ingarden, who saw such indeterminacy as flaws; New Literary History 3(2) 279ff; later in The Implied Reader
practical_applications: Leave the link between Mint's line and Tao's line for the reader to make
limitations: Not read; summary from search snippets

title: Meta-Rhymes in Classical Thai Poetry
key_findings: Chanthalak describe khana (structure), phayang (syllable count), samphat (rhyme); wak -> baat -> bot
External rhyme (samphat nok) compulsory: syllables alike except tone and initial; internal rhyme (samphat nai) optional, where poets show skill; alliteration counts as internal rhyme
Without rhyme a Thai poem 'cannot exist' (Bidyalankarana blank-verse anecdote via Mosel)
All 5 forms (rai, khlong, kap, chan, klon) reduce to 3 couplet meta-patterns; khlong developed from rai; khlong rhymes keep same tone
External rhyme marks rhythmic groups and builds stanzas (ruat yai / ruat lek); rhyme is what makes poetry 'phairo'
practical_applications: Thai two-line dialogue gains 'phairo' from one cross-line vowel rhyme (last word of line 1 -> early word of line 2)
limitations: Scanned 1986 text, transcription garbled in places

title: Thai poetry (Wikipedia)
key_findings: Five forms khlong, chan, kap, klon, rai; chanthalak
Kap yani 11 = 5+6 syllables; kap chabang 16 = 6+4+6; kap surangkhanang 28 = 7x4
Khlong si suphap: mai ek x7, mai tho x4 positions; chan uses heavy/light (khru/lahu) syllables from Pali/Sanskrit metres
Klon: syllables per wak name the metre; klon paet most common in Rattanakosin
practical_applications: Quick lookup of syllable counts only; verify with Thai prosody textbook

title: กลอนสุภาพ กลอนดอกสร้อย กลอนสักวา (TrueplookPanya)
authors: อลงกรณ์ พลอยแก้ว และทีมงานทรูปลูกปัญญา
key_findings: กลอนสุภาพ 1 วรรค 8 คำ (7-9 ได้); 2 วรรค = 1 คำกลอน; 2 คำกลอน = 1 บท
เสียงท้ายวรรค: สดับ ใช้ได้ทุกเสียงแต่ไม่นิยมสามัญ; รับ ห้ามสามัญ/ตรี นิยมจัตวา; รอง/ส่ง นิยมสามัญหรือตรี ห้ามเอก โท จัตวา
สัมผัสนอก (สัมผัสสระ) บังคับ; สัมผัสใน (สระหรือพยัญชนะ) เพิ่มความไพเราะ
practical_applications: Checklist when writing a Thai klon line for a caption
limitations: School-level educational page; other sources phrase tone rules as 'นิยม/ไม่ควร' rather than 'ห้าม'

title: การออกแบบทำนองในการขับร้องเพลงไทยด้วยหลักสัทศาสตร์: กรณีศึกษาเพลง รู้มั้ยจ๊ะ
authors: พิฆาตไพรี พ.
key_findings: Composers avoid melody moving opposite to the lexical tone direction, but exact match on every syllable is not required
High tone (ตรี) tends to be flattened to a level pitch in singing
practical_applications: Thai TTS/sung taglines: avoid pitch contours that contradict word tone, or meaning blurs

title: Literature for Life: The Context and Conditions of Its Emergence in Thailand, 1940s-50s
key_findings: 'Literature for life' (wannakham phuea chiwit) emerged from contests among conservative, liberal and communist writers and critics, 1940s-50s
1970s radical students defined it as literature serving common people and social justice; some called for 'burning' classics
practical_applications: Thai readers have a long tradition of expecting literature to carry social meaning - didactic expectation is cultural, not only a cliché

title: Thai Literary Trends: From Seni Saowaphong to Chart Kobjitti
key_findings: Seni Saowaphong's Ghosts (1953-54) reframes karma as something people act on; 1970s shift from social revolution to inner consciousness after 1976
Chart Korbjitti's The Judgement (1981; SEA Write 1982) critiques attributing suffering to karma and merit-making; existentialist influence
practical_applications: Buddhist concepts in Thai fiction can be questioned, not only preached
limitations: Short essay; novels not short stories

title: The Tale of Khun Chang Khun Phaen: Siam's Great Folk Epic of Love and War
key_findings: First complete English prose translation, based on Prince Damrong's Library Edition plus earlier passages; A. L. Becker translation prize 2010
practical_applications: Reference edition when quoting KCKP in English
limitations: Publisher page and search summaries only

title: Khun Chang Khun Phaen (Wikipedia)
key_findings: Over 20,000 couplets; oral sepha performance from ~17th c.; written in klon (klon paet)
Standard edition 1917-18 (Wachirayan Library, Prince Damrong); some chapters attributed to Rama II, future Rama III, Sunthorn Phu
Feminist critique of Wanthong's portrayal in the 1970s; characters entered everyday speech
practical_applications: Archetype source for Thai love-rivalry stories; handle Wanthong respectfully

title: Sunthorn Phu: Thailand's Beloved Poet
key_findings: Born 1786; UNESCO honoured him as a world poet in 1986; Sunthorn Phu Day 26 June
Phra Aphai Mani named best verse fable, Nirat Phukhao Thong best nirat by the 'Thai Royal Society of Literature' (as the page words it); Nirat Mueang Klaeng
Known for klon paet with rhymes linking across and within lines; easy, memorable language
practical_applications: Model for accessible klon with heavy internal rhyme

title: S.E.A. Write Award (Wikipedia)
key_findings: Annual since 1979; conceived by The Oriental hotel Bangkok, backed by Thai Airways and others
Thai winners include Kampoon Boonthawee (1979), Naowarat Pongpaiboon (1980), Chart Korbjitti (1982, 1994), Angkarn Kalayanapong (1986), Prabda Yoon (2002); 2020 Jadet Kamjorndej
practical_applications: Reading list of Thai short-story/poetry craft
limitations: Tier E; works not listed for early years

title: Haiku Society of America Definitions
key_findings: Haiku: short poem using imagistic language to convey the essence of an experience of nature or the season (linked to the human condition)
Senryu: brief poem highlighting the human condition
5-7-5 'not wrong' but rests on a misunderstanding that Japanese 'on' equal English syllables; a cut suggests a relationship between images
practical_applications: Mint & Tao pair can work like a haiku cut: image line + human line

title: The Long and Short of It: From Aphorism to Novel
key_findings: Short genres each have their own brevity; apothegms (Heraclitus, Laozi, Wittgenstein) leave mystery, dicta (Spinoza, Marx, Freud) claim to solve it
A dictum allows no qualification and applies 'always and everywhere'; witticisms depend on timing
practical_applications: Prefer apothegm-like lines (open question) over dicta (final verdict) to avoid preachiness

title: Quote Origin: For Sale, Baby Shoes, Never Worn
key_findings: No substantive evidence Hemingway wrote it; precursors 1906 (baby carriage ad), 1910 Spokane, 1917 Kane 'Little Shoes, Never Worn', 1921 Moulton
Earliest Hemingway link: De Groot play (1984/1989); Miller 1991 book presents bet as fact
Method: search digitised newspapers/books (Chronicling America, NewspaperArchive, HathiTrust, Google Books), find earliest instance, follow attribution drift
practical_applications: Never caption 'Hemingway's six-word story'; say 'a famous six-word story, often misattributed to Hemingway'

title: How viral misquotes evolve and replicate (interview with Garson O'Toole)
key_findings: Misattribution mechanisms: textual proximity, synthesis and streamlining, proverbial wisdom, real-world proximity, similar names, concoctions
practical_applications: Checklist of how fake quotes are born

title: International Society for the Empirical Study of Literature (IGEL) - About
key_findings: Founded 1987 (Siegfried J. Schmidt, Siegen); promotes empirical study of literature and media; journal Scientific Study of Literature
practical_applications: Where to look for new reader-response evidence

title: Microfiction (draft chapter for The Cambridge Companion to the English Short Story)
key_findings: Terms sudden, flash, quick, micro fiction form a 'polemical field'; history of very short fiction precedes the labels
practical_applications: Word-count labels are conventions, not definitions

title: Ramakien murals, Wat Phra Kaew (Smarthistory) and JSS 'Lacquer Pavilion in its First Reign Context'
authors: Smarthistory; Journal of the Siam Society
key_findings: (per search) Ramakien composed 1797 under Rama I's supervision, partly by him; Rama II rewrote parts for khon
Wat Phra Kaew murals first painted in Rama I's reign, repeatedly restored; murals present Rama as ideal king
practical_applications: Ramakien is shared cultural heritage - reference with respect, not as decoration

title: Aristotle's Aesthetics (Poetics)
authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (author name not captured)
key_findings: Mimesis is central; plot (mythos) is the most important part of tragedy
Plot needs unity and a size that can be held in memory
Peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) are key sources of emotional effect; should follow probability/necessity
Catharsis meaning is disputed (purgation, clarification, consolation, relief)
practical_applications: A 2-line Mint & Tao story = a micro recognition (anagnorisis): line 2 reframes line 1
Do not claim one fixed meaning of catharsis
limitations: Read through a fetch summariser; long entry, only the first ~100k characters were processed
license: copyrighted (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; free to read, not to republish)

title: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (SN 56.11): Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion
key_findings: Middle way avoids two extremes: sensual indulgence and self-affliction
Dukkha (rendered 'stress') includes birth, aging, death, separation from the loved, not getting what one wants; the five clinging-aggregates
Eightfold path: right view, resolve, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration
practical_applications: Middle way in its original sense; any work-life 'balance' use is an analogy and should be framed as such
limitations: Thanissaro renders dukkha as 'stress' — other translators use 'suffering'/'unsatisfactoriness'

title: Anatta-lakkhana Sutta (SN 22.59): The Discourse on the Not-self Characteristic
key_findings: Each aggregate (form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness) is not-self because it leads to affliction and cannot be made to be as one wishes
What is impermanent is unsatisfactory and not fit to be regarded as 'mine, I, my self'
practical_applications: Anatta is about not clinging to aggregates as 'me/mine' — not 'you don't exist'
limitations: Doctrinal; interpretations of anatta differ across schools
license: copyrighted (Buddhist Publication Society); free distribution licence on Access to Insight: copies free of charge, max 50 reprints, credit source, include licence

title: Anger Is Like Grasping a Hot Coal (Quote Investigator)
key_findings: 1988 Borysenko & Rothstein book ascribed the hot-coal analogy directly to the Buddha
practical_applications: Corroborates FBQ_HotCoal

title: The living handbook of narratology - entries 'Narratology' and 'Narrative Constitution'
authors: Jan Christoph Meister; Michael Scheffel (living handbook of narratology, University of Hamburg)
key_findings: Meister, 'Narratology' (rev. 2014): narratology is a humanities discipline dedicated to the study of the logic, principles and practices of narrative representation.

Scheffel, 'Narrative Constitution' (rev. 2013): fabula/sujet comes from Russian formalism (Shklovsky); Tomashevsky: fabula = 'the totality of motifs in their logical causal-temporal chain', sujet = the same motifs in the sequence in which they are presented; later pairs histoire/discours (Todorov), story/plot (Forster).
practical_applications: Separate WHAT happens (fabula) from HOW/ORDER it is told (syuzhet) when planning a clip - the same events can be told as suspense, curiosity or surprise.
limitations: Read via the handbook's print PDFs (archive site).

title: Replication of Kidd & Castano (2013) literary-fiction / theory-of-mind effect (3 labs)
key_findings: Replication of Kidd & Castano (2013, Science) across 3 labs, N = 792: no RMET advantage for literary fiction after one passage.
Lifetime fiction exposure still predicted RMET.
Kidd & Castano disputed it; van Kuijk et al. reported a replication largely consistent with the original - mixed.
practical_applications: Do not claim 'one story makes people more empathic' in content.
limitations: Read via BPS digest and summaries.

title: Poetics (trans. S. H. Butcher), Parts VI and XV
key_findings: Part VI: 'Character is that which reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids'; tragedy is an imitation 'not of men, but of an action and of life'; plot = arrangement of incidents.

Part XV: four aims for character - good, propriety (appropriate to type), true to life, consistent; even an inconsistent model must be 'consistently inconsistent'; speech and action should follow necessity or probability.
practical_applications: Define character by the choices the person makes under pressure, not by a list of adjectives.
Use 'consistently inconsistent' as the rule for erratic characters: the inconsistency itself must be patterned.
limitations: Ancient prescriptive poetics, not empirical; 'propriety' reflects ancient gender/class norms (e.g. manly courage unsuited to a woman) that must not be copied.
license: public domain (translation); MIT Internet Classics Archive

title: Reading Literary Fiction Improves Theory of Mind
key_findings: Five experiments: reading literary fiction (vs nonfiction, popular fiction or nothing) briefly improved affective (and in exps 4-5 cognitive) theory-of-mind test performance.
practical_applications: Historical example of a viral fiction/character claim that later largely failed to replicate.
limitations: Abstract only; see Panero2016, Camerer2018, FORRT_KiddCastano.

title: FLoRA replication atlas entry: Reading Literary Fiction Improves Theory of Mind
authors: FORRT (Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training)
key_findings: Lists 6 replications of Kidd & Castano 2013: Dijkstra et al. 2015 failed, Panero et al. 2016 failed, Samur et al. 2017 failed, van Kuijk et al. 2018 successful (close replication of Exp 5), Kidd & Castano 2018 mixed, Camerer et al. 2018 failed (supplementary Table 4, unsuccessful stage 1).
practical_applications: Quick status check before citing a famous psychology finding.
limitations: Volunteer-curated database; individual replications not all read here.
